source: Direct user clarification in this chat after relaxing the original zero-regression performance rule.
production_target: Large servers, often with access to more than 100 CPUs and abundant RAM. Exact physical-core, logical-CPU and NUMA topology is not yet specified.
primary_objective: More available cores should deliver meaningfully higher end-to-end throughput on representative production workloads.

tradeoffs.performance: Accept measured local slowdowns when a representative end-to-end workload benefits materially; report both gains and costs rather than applying a blanket per-microbenchmark veto.
tradeoffs.memory: Additional working memory may be justified by throughput or accuracy gains. Measure and disclose peak memory and memory per concurrent worker; abundant RAM is not an unlimited budget.
tradeoffs.compatibility: Preserve the original public tdigest_rs API and arithmetic, pinned independent oracle, and untouched original suite. This hardware preference does not authorize silent numerical or wire changes.
tradeoffs.numerics: Quantify and disclose any proposed modern-engine numerical differences by data scale and route, retaining separate rank, value and CDF error checks. Preserve correctness requirements.
tradeoffs.history: Keep all prior benchmark observations and original-policy dispositions unchanged. Reconsideration is a new workload-based evaluation, not retroactive acceptance.

next_validation_priorities: Complete missing validation for E03 and E08, and assess their relevance to worker-result aggregation; E03 targets two-way merges and E08 targets multiway merges. Neither patch itself introduces parallelism or has demonstrated many-core scaling.
Assess E09 capped-merge allocation savings under concurrency. Keep E13 conditional on Python serialization being a material end-to-end cost.
Evaluate retained candidates individually and in combinations with PR #9 before recommending follow-up PRs.

routes: Many independent digests or groups processed concurrently.
One large dataset partitioned across workers, including the cost and numerical effects of merging worker results.
Mixed production-style workloads including ingestion, merge, query, serialization and language-boundary costs.
scaling_plan.worker_counts: Use increasing available worker counts, for example 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128, restricted to actual allocated hardware; report physical cores, SMT, quotas and topology separately.
scaling_plan.dataset_sizes: Measure both fixed-total-data completion time and throughput as data grows with worker count. Include skewed groups and unequal shards.
metrics: End-to-end records per second and elapsed time
Speedup and throughput per allocated core
Peak resident memory, memory per worker and allocation activity
Accuracy, mass, extrema, state and wire behavior across worker counts and merge orders
scaling_plan.execution: All library builds, tests and benchmarks remain on Linux/WSL. Benchmark fixed input/settings with controlled repeated baseline/candidate runs. Investigate memory bandwidth, NUMA placement, lock contention, Python GIL boundaries and nested thread-pool oversubscription as applicable.
scaling_plan.threading_policy: Design configurable concurrency that can cooperate with caller-managed pools. Parallel execution must not silently replace the original arithmetic path.
scaling_plan.evidence_limit: Existing local single-worker results do not establish performance or scaling on a server with more than 100 CPUs. No such measurement has been made by recording this preference.

execution_status: Preference and next-validation plan recorded only. No new builds, benchmarks, code changes, PR changes or automation started in this update.
